results.title: Azure VM Price Change - Microsoft Q&A
highlights:
2026-10-05T00:37:46.26+00:00 

Price change below will be affected if we have valid Azure VM Reservation or the new price will be applied when reservation was expired?

 Answer accepted by question author 

 2026-10-05T01:24:20.01+00:00 

Hi, 

Existing VM Reserved Instances (RIs) will not be affected by the price increase. Reserved Instances are a pre-purchase of the base VM costs (even if you choose monthly), which is why the price is locked in for the entire 1 or 3 year term. Please see below screenshot from portal:

If you purchase or renew an RI after the price increase takes effect then the purchase price will be higher than it is now for the listed regions and affected VM sizes. Also, if you allow reservation to expire and don't renew/purchase new then the new full Pay-As-You-Go price that is in effect for that region/VM size will apply.

Please let me know if you have any questions.

...

For Azure VM reservations, the reservation discount continues through the committed term. Existing reservations remain valid through their term and continue providing discounts for eligible usage.

When the reservation expires, usage moves to pay-as-you-go rates unless another commitment option is selected. For reservations with autorenew turned on, a replacement reservation is purchased automatically when the reservation expires. If autorenew is off, the billing discount expires and resources are billed at the pay-as-you-go price.

So, a VM price increase does not change the discount on an active reservation during its valid term. The new pricing matters when the reservation expires and the workload falls back to pay-as-you-go, or when a new reservation or renewal is purchased under the then-current pricing.

results.title: Request for a Cost-Effective Azure GPU VM Equivalent to NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080 (16 GB) - Microsoft Q&A
highlights:
# Request for a Cost-Effective Azure GPU VM Equivalent to NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080 (16 GB)

 Abrar Adil S 476 Reputation points 

 2026-10-26T18:02:31.67+00:00 

We have a requirement to host an application on Azure that specifies the following hardware configuration:

Processor: Intel Core Ultra 9 285K

Memory: 64 GB RAM

Storage: 1 TB SSD

Graphics: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080 (16 GB VRAM)

We initially considered the Azure VM size `Standard_NC24lds_xl_RTXPRO6000BSE_v6`, which provides a 1/4 allocation of the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU with 24 GB of GPU memory. However, the estimated cost is significantly higher than our budget. We need to identify a cost-effective Azure solution that can meet its requirements. An exact RTX 5080 equivalent is not mandatory if a compatible alternative can be recommended.

...

2026-10-26T21:17:28.3366667+00:00 

Hello Abrar Adil S, 

Thank you for reaching out to us on the Microsoft Q&A forum and for providing the application requirements. 

Azure does not currently provide virtual machines with a consumer NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080 GPU. Azure GPU virtual machines use datacenter or professional GPUs, so there is no direct one-to-one Azure VM equivalent based only on the GPU model or its 16 GB VRAM.

Based on the stated requirements, the first lower-cost Azure VM I would recommend evaluating is:

Standard NC16as T4_v3

This size provides:

- 16 vCPUs
- 110 GiB system memory
- One NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU
- 16 GB of GPU memory
- Support for CUDA-based workloads
- Support for GPU-accelerated OpenGL and DirectX applications
- Support for Azure managed disks

A separate 1 TiB Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2, or another suitable managed disk can be attached to meet the storage requirement.

However, the NVIDIA T4 is not performance-equivalent to the GeForce RTX 5080. It is an older GPU and may provide substantially lower performance for workloads that depend on newer CUDA capabilities, advanced rendering, ray tracing, OptiX, Vulkan, or high graphics throughput. Therefore, `Standard_NC16as_T4_v3` should be treated as a cost-effective compatibility candidate, not as a guaranteed substitute.

If the application is primarily an interactive graphics, CAD, 3D visualization, rendering, or virtual-workstation application, also review the NVadsA10_v5 series. It uses NVIDIA A10 GPUs and includes NVIDIA GRID licensing.

...

Check whether `Standard_NC16as_T4_v3` is available and has quota in the intended Azure region.

...

Deploy one temporary test VM with the required operating system.
3. Install the Azure-supported NVIDIA CUDA or GRID driver appropriate for the workload.

...

Attach the required 1 TiB managed disk.

...

If the T4 does not meet the required performance or feature level, the next step would be to evaluate an A10-based VM or retain the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell-based option. Pricing, quota, and VM availability should be verified for the intended region through the Azure portal or Azure Pricing Calculator because they vary by region and agreement.

results.title: Email Received - Microsoft Q&A
highlights:
I have received this email. I dont know how this is going to affect our billing 

You're receiving this notification because you're associated with one or more Azure subscriptions that use Standard SSD for managed disk transactions. For reference, you can find this notification in the Azure portal under Service Health/ Health advisories using tracking ID: MQR7-KK0. 

Starting on 3 December 2026*,* we’ll be changing the maximum paid transactions per hour for Standard SSD managed disk transactions. This change reflects ongoing improvements in our product portfolio and better aligns with evolving workload patterns. 

How do i know what disk I am paying for ?

...

Hi,

You can see list of Disks for your current subscription using below link in Azure portal:

https://portal.azure.com/#view/Microsoft_Azure_StorageHub/StorageHub.MenuView/~/DisksBrowse

Check Storage type column, and see if any are Standard SSD. These are the disks that the email applies to.

For LRS, they have doubled the maximum hourly paid transactions. If you take a look at Managed Disk pricing page, scroll down to Standard SSD pricing chart (SKUs begin with E, e.g. E1,E2,E3,E4,E6,etc.), then look at the Max transaction price per month (this is what could double in worst case), and the Max total price per month columns.

The prices that are on pricing page now are the current prices, not the new prices.

What you are charged depends on how many transactions you are performing on your Standard SSD disk(s). If you constantly have lots of transactions (read,write,etc.) then you will see an increase.

For example, say you have 128GiB Standard LRS SSD in East US. The current monthly max total price at Pay-As-You-Go pricing would be $31.10. After December 3 the monthly max total price would be $52.60.

Please keep in mind most people do not use maximum transactions in my experience. That is typically only if you have very IO-heavy workload that is constantly busy all month.

results.title: 1,000x Overcharge Bug on "Qwen38 27b SFT Gl 1M Tokens" (44K tokens billed as 44M tokens) - Microsoft Q&A
highlights:
2026-10-29T03:34:32.78+00:00

...

I ran a small Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) job on qwen3.8-27b (Global training tier) in eastus2.

Although the Microsoft Foundry portal explicitly confirms that only 44,000 tokens (0.044M tokens) were billed, Azure Cost Management recorded the usage quantity as 44 (44M tokens) against a 1M token meter, resulting in an exact 1,000x overcharge ($132.00 USD instead of $0.132 USD).

I opened a Billing Support request (SR #2610200010000024), but the vendor support team insists that because 44 × $3.00 = $132.00, the invoice math is "valid," and they refuse to investigate the metering pipeline bug unless I purchase a paid Technical Support plan.

- Tokens Billed in Foundry UI (Expected): 44,000 tokens (0.044M tokens)
- Quantity Recorded in Azure Billing (Actual): 44 (44,000,000 tokens / 44M tokens) — 1,000x unit conversion bug
- Expected Charge: $0.132 USD (¥20.80 JPY)
- Actual Billed Charge: $132.00 USD (¥20,796.60 JPY / displayed as ¥20,797)
- Overcharged Amount: +$131.87 USD (+¥20,775.80 JPY)

...

2. Official Azure Retail Prices API (eastus2) The new meter (effective October 1, 2026) is priced per 1M tokens with tierMinimumUnits set to 0.0:

- meterName: Qwen38 27b SFT Gl 1M Tokens
- meterId: 59a176f8-721a-5e7d-954a-250a4e3a5e3d
- skuId: DZH318Z0SDFC/01PV
- armRegionName: eastus2
- unitOfMeasure: 1M
- unitPrice: 3.0 USD
- tierMinimumUnits: 0.0
- effectiveStartDate: 2026-10-01T00:00:00Z

3. Actual Usage Record from Microsoft.Consumption/usageDetails API Unlike older fine-tuning meters (such as Qwen3 32B FT Tokens) which are billed per 1K tokens, Qwen38 27b SFT Gl 1M Tokens is billed per 1M tokens. However, the metering pipeline emitted the 1K-scaled value (44) directly into the 1M meter:

- date: 2026-10-19T00:00:00Z
- meterName: Qwen38 27b SFT Gl 1M Tokens
- meterId: 59a176f8-721a-5e7d-954a-250a4e3a5e3d
- quantity: 44
- unitOfMeasure: 1M
- effectivePrice: 3
- costInUSD: 132
- costInBillingCurrency: 20796.6

...

Based on the records provided, this strongly indicates a metering unit conversion defect rather than valid consumption. The Foundry-reported 44,000 billable training tokens equal `0.044` units on a meter whose unit is one million tokens:

`44,000 / 1,000,000 × $3.00 = $0.132`

Recording a quantity of `44` against that meter produces `$132.00`, which is exactly 1,000 times higher. Microsoft’s fine-tuning documentation confirms that SFT training is token-based and that rates expressed per million tokens must be calculated using the token count divided by 1,000,000: Manage fine-tuning costs.

results.title: Azure GPU virtual machines vs standalone Docker containers for AMD/NVIDIA game streaming research - Microsoft Q&A
highlights:
My total budget is approximately €150 for short academic benchmarking sessions, so consumption-based billing would be preferable.

...

Short version for your dissertation design: Azure has one managed option for GPU containers without VMs or Kubernetes, and it only covers half of your matrix.

Azure Container Apps serverless GPUs run standalone containers on a GPU, with no VM or cluster for you to manage, per-second billing and scale to zero. The limits that matter for you:

- NVIDIA only: T4 and A100. There's no AMD GPU option, so the AMD Radeon container environment can't be built this way.
- West Europe has T4 only, and you need a new workload-profiles environment there to add it. A100 is in regions such as Sweden Central and Italy North.
- Compute-focused: Microsoft's docs mention CUDA, and list rendering and video transcoding as example scenarios. They don't document Vulkan/OpenGL display rendering or NVENC access inside the container. A game-streaming stack (Steam/Proton plus Sunshine) needs both, so test that early before you build the experiment around it.
- One container per replica gets the GPU, and fractional GPUs aren't supported.
- Container Apps doesn't run privileged containers, so Tailscale would need its userspace networking mode rather than a TUN device.
- If you need Docker Engine itself in the comparison (not just an OCI image), that means a GPU VM running Docker.

For the AMD side (Radeon PRO V710/V620), Azure only offers GPU VMs, so the "AMD Docker container" leg would have to run on a VM you manage. If your method allows it, one fair option is to run both the VM and the container variants on the same GPU VM size, so the only variable is the runtime layer. With a €150 budget, run the VMs only during benchmark sessions and deallocate them straight after, since a stopped-but-allocated VM keeps billing.

Regarding Azure Storage, the pricing adjustment applies to specific Azure Storage services and SKUs rather than generally to all services associated with a StorageV2 (general-purpose v2) account.

results.title: i got charged 3 times for a managed compute environment - Microsoft Q&A
highlights:
2026-10-11T18:50:01.1266667+00:00 

i got charged 3 times (according to the invoice) for some managed compute envirinment/service, but i have no idea how that happened. I was exploring foundry, couldn't get anything to work and i left. Few days later i got charged for something i had no idea was about to charge me. Basic ai support can't seem to be of any help. Any ideas how to go about refunding it (i never used these services)?

...

this can happen with Foundry, especially if u accidentally created a managed compute deployment while experimenting with models. Unlike pay-per-token models, managed compute can charge for allocated GPU capacity even when nobody is actually using the model. So not sending any requests doesn't necessarily mean there won't be charges.

First, I'd check Cost Management + Billing > Cost analysis and group the charges by Resource and Meter. That should help identify what was actually billed. Three entries on an invoice don't automatically mean u were charged three times for the same thing. They could represent different usage periods, resources, or billing meters.

Also check ur Foundry deployments and any Azure Machine Learning managed online endpoints. If something is still deployed, delete it to stop further compute charges. Just closing Foundry or leaving the project unused won't necessarily stop billing. For the refund, open an Azure Billing support request through Help + support. Billing support is free, even without a paid support plan. Explain that u were exploring Foundry, didn't realize a billable compute resource had been provisioned, and never intentionally used the service. Ask for a one-time courtesy refund or billing adjustment.

Include the invoice number, three charge amounts, resource IDs, and the dates involved. Microsoft can review the actual usage and decide whether a refund is possible, but it's not guaranteed.
